column1: # tests/budgets.tsv - Q6: performance budgets, and where each came from.
# One row per measurement the kernel emits as a `[perf] name value unit`
# line. tools/qemu-serial-test.sh reads this and fails the run when a
# Every number here is a CEILING with stated headroom over a MEASURED
# value, in the same discipline SECONDS_TO_RUN's comment history in
# qemu-serial-test.sh already applies to itself. The `measured` and
# `commit` columns are what make a failure diagnosable: "the disk got
# three times slower since b7bb520" is a starting point, "too slow" is
# A budget that has sat at 2x slack for ten milestones is a bug in the
# budget. Re-measure and tighten it, and say so here when you do.
# These were measured on QEMU's TCG under macOS on Apple Silicon. There is
# no hosted runner behind them and there is not meant to be one: they are a
# claim about that machine. Measured somewhere else they will move - an
# Intel Mac is somewhere else, and under -accel hvf it is not even the same
# kind of measurement - and moving them with a recorded reason is the
# Q18: the `input_to_photon_*_{best,med,worst}` rows replaced a single
# number that swung 3x between consecutive runs of the same image. The
# `measured` column for those six is now a real observation, and the
# first one taught something the single number could not: within one
# boot the idle path is tight (40757 / 42303 / 43475 us - a 7% spread),
# while the loaded worst frame is twice the loaded median (81547 against
# 40742). So the 3x swing that motivated this milestone was *between*
# boots, not within one, and it is the boot conditions that vary rather
# than the path. That is a different problem, it is now visible, and it
# is what these rows exist to keep visible.

column6: M117: 362 -> 405-423 across the graded boots of M111-M117 (the package manager's, the browser's and M117's own self-tests; the browser install alone adds [m113]'s checks and the `os preinstall` on first boot). Ceiling unchanged at 600 - still 1.4x. M100 (fifth increment): 223 -> 362, and all of it is the library stack's own suites - expat's 4,392 checks are 55 s of it, sqlite 3 s, freetype 1.5 s; see those rows. The ceiling stays at 600, which is now 1.65x rather than 2.7x, and qemu-serial-test.sh's capture ceiling was raised to match. The full self-test boot. Dominated by tests that spawn a process and wait for it, so it is variable rather than merely large - the ceiling is set against a busy host, not a quiet one. An ordinary boot with self-tests off is ~8s and is not this number. M102 moved the measured value from 192 s to 223 s on purpose: its self-test exhausts the machine's physical memory twice, and on the 4 GiB configuration that is about a million page faults per round. The ceiling did not move - there is still most of it spare - but the measured column has to say what a run now costs, or the next person to add thirty seconds will think they added five.

1 MiB through virtio-blk, cache dropped first. The README quotes 5.6 ms for virtio and 95 ms for the ATA PIO fallback; the ceiling covers both paths plus headroom, because QEMU_DISK=ide runs the same marker.
The same megabyte out of M92's write-through cache. Generous headroom on purpose: this is a memcpy whose cost is dominated by whatever else the host is doing.
Cursor motion to a changed pixel, TSC-measured, on an idle machine. M69's own note says the observer competes, so this is an upper bound rather than a measurement of the path alone.
The same, with CPU-bound tasks running. The number that matters for "does the desktop stay usable under load", and the one most sensitive to the host.
Q18: the shape rather than a sample. The best case is what the path costs when nothing is in the way.
Q18: what it usually costs. This is the row a regression in the ordinary path moves.
Q18: what a person actually notices. A desktop is judged by its worst frames, so this is the row with an opinion in it.
Q18: as above, with CPU-bound tasks running.
Q18: the median under load.
Q18: the worst frame under load, which is the number that decides whether the desktop stays usable. Deliberately the widest here: it is also the noisiest, and a different host will move it.

M101: what one `int 0x80` round trip costs, measured with SYS_getpid - a call that does almost nothing, so what is left is the trap, the dispatch and the return. This is the number the `syscall`/`sysret` deferral has been waiting for since M69. The ceiling is ~4x a measurement that moved between 1020 and 1300 cycles across three boots of the same image, because it is a cycle count taken on a virtualised TSC and it is the noisiest row here; what it is for is catching a trap path that has become an order of magnitude slower, not policing jitter.

M104: 1 MiB written block by block into the writeback cache and then barriered to the disk. The ceiling is the same as the cold READ's, because the write path can never be cheaper than the read it is measured against and this is a regression ceiling rather than a target.

M104: the same megabyte a sector at a time, which is the write-through path. Kept as a row because it is the denominator of the writeback ratio - a run where these two converge is a run where writeback stopped absorbing anything, and that is the regression this catches.
M104: 1 MiB read sequentially with readahead off, which is the default. The pair below is the measurement that chose that default.

M104: the same read with eight lines fetched ahead. Slower, and the row exists so that the day it stops being slower - a smaller filesystem block, a device where a byte costs more than a request - the number says so rather than somebody arguing about it.

M105: the full scan an unclean mount runs - every allocated inode's block tree walked, a shadow bitmap built, the two compared - over the ordinary boot filesystem, with the block cache dropped first. Cold on purpose: a mount scan runs because the machine was NOT shut down cleanly, so it always runs on a just-booted machine. Measured warm the same scan swung 4747 to 25476 us across two boots, which is a measurement of the run before it. This is the row M71's second condition - "a full scan gets slow" - is decided by. M105 set the ceiling at 100 ms as an opinion about where a mount stops being instant, measured 6 ms, and concluded the cost does not move with the file count. M97 moved it to 128 ms and the row failed, which is the row doing its job: eighty megabytes of C++ runtime and test binaries went onto the image, and the scan walks every allocated inode's block tree, so the INDIRECT BLOCKS it reads scale with total data rather than with the number of files. M105's "does not move with the file count" is still true and was the wrong thing to measure. The ceiling is 400 ms now, set from the measurement rather than from an opinion, and what it watches is a scan whose cost has changed SHAPE - see M105's amendment. M98 repeated M97's move at twice the size: the native toolchain - cc1, cc1plus, libstdc++'s headers, the sysroot, GNU make - is another ~160 MB of allocated blocks, and the scan went 128 ms to 711 ms, linear in bytes exactly as the M97 sentence above predicts. Ceiling re-set from the new measurement with the same ~2x headroom. Checked against M105's restated journal condition on the way: the scan is CPU-walking resident structures over cached blocks, not disk-bound, so the condition still does not fire - but this row is now the closest thing to it, and the next multiple of growth lands it near a second, which is where M105 said a mount stops being instant. M100 (second increment): the ceiling failed, and what it found is worth more than the row. 3.5 MiB of libpng and libjpeg - 1.4% more allocated bytes - moved this number 90%, from 904 ms to 1714 ms, reproducibly, on freshly built images either way. That is not linear in bytes and the sentence above is now known to be wrong about the mechanism. The scan gained block-layer counters in the same increment, and they say what it is: 79512 block reads, only 311 of which miss the cache, and 2936 sectors to the device. The scan is memcpy-bound in the block cache, not disk-bound - map_block re-reads a whole 4 KiB indirect table for every logical block of every file, so walking 251 MiB of image copies about 320 MiB, at about 18 us a cached read. Ceiling re-set from six measurements spanning 1416-1716 ms with the usual ~2x headroom, and a new row (mount_scan_repeat_us) sits beside it. KNOWN AND UNEXPLAINED: mount_scan_busy_us runs the same walk with the same three counters and costs HALF - 780 ms against 1550 - and a synthetic fixed-work probe (20000 cached blk_reads) measures 368 ms before the writers and 367 ms after, so the machine does not change between them. Ruled out: the host page cache (a freshly copied image measures the same), first-run warm-up (five back-to-back repeats are all slow), and a process having run (a scan after spawning /bin/hello is still slow). It is reproduced on every boot and it is not explained. M165 (fourth increment, and the row behaving exactly as written): the three rows failed together at 3008368/3000006/2994028 us against a 3000000 ceiling, which reads like a regression in the fork and TLB-shootdown work committed beside it and is not one. The scan's own counters settle it: 309592 block reads, 531 of them missing the cache, 5400 sectors to the device - IDENTICAL before and after that change, on the same image, so the walk did not grow by one read. What grew is the disk. M100 recorded 79512 block reads for the 1555000 beside this row; this image does 309592, 3.9x as many, because M155 through M165 put Chromium on it - /bin/chromiumcontent alone is 329 MB, and chromiumblink, chromiumv8, chromiumcc2 and the rest are beside it. Linear in allocated bytes is what this row has said since M97 and it is still saying it. Re-set from six measurements spanning 2994028-3049674 us with the same ~2x headroom. Two things worth keeping: the numbers above were taken on a host whose cpptools sat at 35-61% of a core indexing the Chromium checkout for the whole session and never went quiet, so the 1.4% spread across those six is not a clean measurement and the ceiling is deliberately not set tight against it; and mount_scan_busy_us has stopped costing HALF the quiet scan - it is now within 2% of it, so the unexplained thing the row below describes has gone away at this size rather than been explained.

M105: the same scan, run again immediately, cold both times. M100's second increment is why this row exists. 3.5 MiB of libpng and libjpeg went on the image - 1.4% more allocated bytes - and mount_scan_us went 904 ms to 1714 ms, reproducibly, on freshly built images either way, against a row whose own note above says the cost is linear in allocated bytes. It is not. The scan grew counters at the same time (see the [m105] line beside these), and they say the walk is IDENTICAL either way to the block read: 79512 block reads, 311 of them missing the cache, 2936 sectors reaching the device. So the scan is not disk-bound and never was - 79201 of those reads are 4 KiB memcpys out of the block cache at about 18 us each, which is the whole measurement, because map_block re-reads a whole indirect table for every logical block of every file. This row is here because it FALSIFIED the obvious explanation: if the first scan of a boot were paying for the host serving the image cold, this one would be fast. It is not - five back-to-back repeats all land within 5% of the first, and an image freshly copied to a new file on the host measures the same. Ceiling set from six measurements (1416-1716 ms) with the usual ~2x headroom. M165 (fourth increment, and the row behaving exactly as written): the three rows failed together at 3008368/3000006/2994028 us against a 3000000 ceiling, which reads like a regression in the fork and TLB-shootdown work committed beside it and is not one. The scan's own counters settle it: 309592 block reads, 531 of them missing the cache, 5400 sectors to the device - IDENTICAL before and after that change, on the same image, so the walk did not grow by one read. What grew is the disk. Linear in allocated bytes is what this row has said since M97 and it is still saying it. Re-set from six measurements spanning 2994028-3049674 us with the same ~2x headroom. M105: the same scan after four concurrent writers have added and deleted several hundred files. Same ceiling, and the pair is still the measurement - but what it says changed when M97 put eighty megabytes of C++ on the image. The two numbers stay close to each other, which is the original point (adding files does not add scan time), and BOTH moved twenty-fold, which is the new one (adding bytes does). See M105's amendment and the note on the row above. M98: both moved together again, ~5.5x, for the row above's reason. M100 (second increment): raised to 3000000 with the row above and for the same reason, and the evidence that it was needed came from the I/O APIC boot rather than the default one. Through the I/O APIC this row measures 1517430 us on cdbca6e's kernel with the same image - already over the old 1500000 ceiling before this increment touched anything - and 1518777, 1519660 and 1569614 on this one. M103 measured the I/O APIC path at about 2x the 8259 one, and this row is 2x. The 780000 beside it is the DEFAULT path's number, which is the one that moved least. And there is something here nobody has explained: through the 8259 this scan costs HALF the quiet scan above it, identical walk and identical block-layer counters, every boot; through the I/O APIC the two are equal (1.52 s against 1.65 s). So it is the busy scan that is environment-dependent and the quiet one that is stable, which is the opposite of what the pair was set up to show. M165 (fourth increment, and the row behaving exactly as written): the three rows failed together at 3008368/3000006/2994028 us against a 3000000 ceiling, which reads like a regression in the fork and TLB-shootdown work committed beside it and is not one. The scan's own counters settle it: 309592 block reads, 531 of them missing the cache, 5400 sectors to the device - IDENTICAL before and after that change, on the same image, so the walk did not grow by one read. What grew is the disk. M100 recorded 79512 block reads for the 1555000 beside this row; this image does 309592, 3.9x as many, because M155 through M165 put Chromium on it - /bin/chromiumcontent alone is 329 MB, and chromiumblink, chromiumv8, chromiumcc2 and the rest are beside it. Linear in allocated bytes is what this row has said since M97 and it is still saying it. Re-set from six measurements spanning 2994028-3049674 us with the same ~2x headroom. Two things worth keeping: the numbers above were taken on a host whose cpptools sat at 35-61% of a core indexing the Chromium checkout for the whole session and never went quiet, so the 1.4% spread across those six is not a clean measurement and the ceiling is deliberately not set tight against it; and mount_scan_busy_us has stopped costing HALF the quiet scan - it is now within 2% of it, so the unexplained thing the row below describes has gone away at this size rather than been explained.

M105: four processes creating, writing, fsyncing, renaming and deleting concurrently through one coarse filesystem lock. Wide on purpose - it is four processes on a virtualised disk and it moved 267 ms to 321 ms across three boots. What it guards is not throughput but liveness: a change that makes two writers serialise pathologically, or deadlock, shows up here as a run that never finishes rather than as a slow one.

M106: one kernel task doing a fixed amount of pure computation - no syscall, no allocation, no filesystem, so what is timed is "can a runnable task get a core" rather than some subsystem's lock. It is the denominator of the row below and it exists so that a change in the ratio can be attributed to one side or the other. Measured on one core; on four the same task costs about 18600 us, because it competes with less.

M106: the same work times the core count, started together and timed until the last one finishes. On one core this IS the row above (one core, one task). On four cores it was 20068 us for four times the work.

M106: the pair above as a ratio, and the row that decides this milestone's remaining bullets. 100 means N times the work cost what one task cost - the work went wide. N*100 means one core did all of it. Measured at 94 on one core and at 129, 155 and 200 across three four-core runs on a quiet host (400 would be fully serialised), which is why per-CPU run queues and work stealing are NOT built: the single sched_lock is not what stops this machine using its cores, and M69's rule is that performance work on an unmeasured path does not get done here. The ceiling is set at 250 so that a four-core run which has started serialising fails, and a one-core run cannot.

M106: the most task slots ever live at once this boot, against MAX_TASKS of 128. A budget rather than a report, and the ceiling is the point: M106's bullet asked for MAX_TASKS "raised to whatever a parallel build actually asks for" and added that the number is "set by the failure, not by rounding up". Nine of 128 is not a failure. This row is what turns "raise it" from a guess into an event - at 100 of 128 the headroom is gone and the number says so before a spawn starts failing.

M106: the most descriptors held at once by any single task, against MAX_FDS of 128. Same argument as the row above. The hungriest task on an ordinary boot is the compositor at around 52 during M50's kill storm and 12 at rest; 128 has never been approached.

M98: one C translation unit (bzip2's bzlib.c, 1,572 lines) compiled by this machine's own gcc, measured by tools/bootstrap-test.sh rather than by the boot battery - it is a build, it takes minutes, and it has its own fw_cfg switch. The ceiling is ~4x a measurement that is itself 128x what the same compile costs on the host QEMU runs on: what it guards is a return of the two things M98 found and fixed - an allocator that was quadratic in live allocations, and a stdio with no write buffer - either of which shows up here as a multiple rather than as a percentage.

M98: the peak resident set of that compile, which is the first memory number this kernel has ever been able to report (kernel/memory_management/virtual_memory.c counts resident pages per address space; getrusage's ru_maxrss carries it out). The ceiling is 128 MiB, which is the smallest machine this project supports booting - a C compile that stops fitting on it is a fact worth failing a run for.

M98: one header- and template-heavy C++ translation unit through cc1plus - the right proxy for "the largest translation unit", because GCC is a C++ program and its own worst files are C++ files. It was 919 s before this milestone's malloc and stdio fixes and failed in the assembler; the ceiling is set against the number after them with the usual margin.

M98: the number M102's swap decision waited on. 217 MiB against the 4 GiB this machine is configured with - and it would fit on the 128 MiB configuration too. The ceiling is 512 MiB: past that, a single compile no longer fits the small machine, which is exactly the condition M102 said would reopen swap.

M98: bzip2 1.0.8 built serially by this machine's own make, gcc, as, ar, ranlib and ld from bzip2's own Makefile - eight translation units, an archive, two links. The end-to-end number for "can this machine build somebody else's program", and the one a regression in any of those six tools moves.

M98: bzip2's OWN test suite, run on this machine against binaries this machine built - three compressions and three decompressions compared with reference files nobody here produced. Fast, and here as a budget rather than only as a pass because a sudden multiple would mean the compressor this machine built got slower, which is a thing no marker would say.

M99: what tests/python/m99.py costs from spawn to exit - an 8 KB PIE, /lib/ld-lean.so relocating it and libpython3.12.so, the startup modules, `import json` read as .py source out of /usr/lib/python3.12 and compiled, and _socket and array dlopen'ed out of lib-dynload. It is the first program on this machine whose start is dominated by small reads rather than by one big one, which is why it is worth a row at all. **It got faster when it became dynamic** - 4400 ms to 3640 ms - and that is the opposite of what a loader is usually assumed to cost: the static interpreter demand-paged 12 MB of one file whether or not a byte of it was reached, and the dynamic one pages in only the part of libpython3.12.so it touches plus the two extension modules it imports. The ceiling is ~5x the measured value rather than the usual 2x, and deliberately: this number will move the day a .pyc cache exists, and it should be re-measured and tightened then rather than left wide.

M100 (fourth increment): tests/freetype/ftrender.c on this machine - DejaVu Sans opened through this libc's stdio stream, and 570 glyphs rendered through freetype's TrueType interpreter, its smooth and monochrome rasterizers and its autohinter, every bitmap hashed. Integer arithmetic in somebody else's code, compiled by this project's compiler, and the ceiling is ~2x the one measurement because the run that produced it was also the run that proved the output byte-identical with the host.

M100 (fourth increment): expat's own tests/runtests - 4,392 checks - from spawn to exit on this machine. Fifty seconds, which is about 100x what the host takes and is the usual TCG ratio rather than anything this OS is doing: the suite allocates and frees a parser per check, so what it grades on the way is this libc's malloc under churn. The ceiling is ~2x. It is the single most expensive self-test in the boot, and if the battery's SECONDS_TO_RUN ever needs raising, this row is why.

M100 (fifth increment): tests/sqlite/cases.sql through /bin/sqlite3 on this machine, from spawn to exit - 5,000 rows inserted through a recursive CTE, an index built over them, a transaction rolled back and one committed through a journal file this filesystem creates, syncs and unlinks, joins, window functions, a VACUUM that rewrites the file, two integrity checks, and a popen and a system() from the shell. Every statement takes fcntl record locks on the way. The ceiling is ~2x the one measurement; the number to watch if the block cache or the lock table ever changes. M107 (2026-09-12): this row is BIMODAL, not noisy, and that is the new fact. M121 left it open with an explicit condition - one run with nothing else on the machine, `ps -Ao pid,ppid,command | grep qemu-system` empty before it starts. M107 met that condition FOUR times, once per storage backend, with the host verified quiet (one VM, no cpptools indexing, no sibling worktree), and the row read 8060 (virtio), 7820 (AHCI), and comparable figures through NVMe and ATA. So it is NOT the second VM M121 suspected. It is also not M107: the same row read 7420-8820 at commit 454cf0d earlier the same day, on a tree containing none of M107's work. build/perf-history.tsv holds the whole shape - every measurement at every commit before 2026-09-12 is 2000-3000 ms, and every measurement on that day is either ~2300 or ~8000, on old and new code alike. Two modes, not a spread, so there is a mechanism and it is environmental rather than random. M133 FOUND IT, and it was neither environmental nor random: flush_all_locked wrote one 4 KiB line per device call, so an fsync of a file holding N dirty lines cost N round trips at ~2.5 ms each. sqlite in autocommit fsyncs several times per statement, which is why a six-row INSERT cost more than a five-thousand-row recursive CTE - the cost was per transaction, not per row. The two modes were whether the file's dirty lines happened to be laid out contiguously enough to be written together, which leanfs allocation decides at create time; the same code on a differently allocated file is a different number. Coalescing contiguous dirty lines into one device_write took the row from 8540 to 2600 ms with the same sectors written. The ceiling was never raised. THE CEILING IS DELIBERATELY NOT RAISED, for M121's reason: a number is a claim, and raising a ceiling to make a run green is how a budget stops being one. What changed here is that the most likely explanation has been eliminated by measurement rather than argued about.

M100 (sixth increment): tests/harfbuzz/hbshape.c on this machine - DejaVu Sans opened by harfbuzz's own loader and again by freetype, and six strings in five scripts shaped through both, twelve runs in all, every glyph and position printed. Mostly the 45 MB static binary demand-paging in and harfbuzz walking the font's GSUB and GPOS tables the first time; the ceiling is ~2x the one measurement.

M100 (eighth increment): the [m100f] TLS fixture from spawn to exit - mbedtls's ssl_server2 started (it seeds a DRBG and parses three certificates before it listens, which is most of the 8-second wait the fixture gives it), its own ssl_client2 completing a verified TLS 1.3 session on loopback, and two runs of the httpsget written here (one that verifies against the CA file and one refused for the wrong name). Every byte over M66's TCP and M100's blocking sockets, the DRBGs seeded from kernel/device/random.c. ~2.6x headroom because a handshake's cost on TCG is dominated by the public-key work, which is the part that varies most between runs.

M100 (eighth increment): the [m100g] three suites (ChaCha20-Poly1305, SHA-2, ECDSA) from spawn to exit - about 720 of mbedtls's own vectors, the ECDSA ones being the expensive part. ~2.2x headroom; this is the row to raise if more suites are added to the [m100g] set.

M98's third box, and the first run that ever produced it. The box asked how close a build on this machine comes to MAX_TASKS, and the answer has never been recorded because tools/bootstrap-test.sh has never reached the end of its own script - `make -j4` does not return, and until M100 bounded it with `measure -t` it took the harness's ceiling with it, so the kernel never printed this line. 9 of 128, which is the same number M98's table in the archive reports and is an order of magnitude below what that milestone predicted. The ceiling is 100 rather than something near 9 for the reason peak_live_tasks' is: this row's job is to fire while there is still headroom, not to track the workload. NOTE the measurement is taken on a build whose -j4 step spins rather than compiles (see build_bzip2_j4_peak_rss_kib), so 9 is what a build that never got four compilers running costs; the day -j4 works, this number should move and that is the news, not a regression.
M98's third box, other half, and first produced in M100 for the reason the row above gives. 4 of 128 in the hungriest task. Same ceiling and the same argument: headroom, not workload.

M116: 256 KiB from the HOST through QEMU's SLIRP, the RTL8139's receive ring and TCP, read to end of stream by /bin/netrecv over the POSIX sockets libcurl uses - spawn to exit, measured by the [m116] self-test. The first number this project has for its receive path through the real NIC. Before M116 the same stream corrupted ~36 frames on the ring and cost about a minute of retransmission; with the ring fixed it was 1119 ms, of which 980 were a first SYN dropped while ARP resolved (now held, arp_hold) - so this row also guards that. The ceiling is ~5x the measurement and sits deliberately below the two regressions it exists for: a FIN ignored when it arrives with data costs 1.4 s, a dropped first packet 1 s. Under hvf it was 17.4 s at 4 GiB and 68 s at 16 GiB, none of it this machine's: SLIRP forks the stream's `cat`, and on macOS that fork stopped the whole VM for ~4.3 s per GiB the guest had touched, until the harnesses shared the guest's RAM (tools/nic-stream-env.sh); tools/nic-stream-test.sh holds this same ceiling on the host's own accelerator at 4 and 16 GiB.

M117: a press on a wm_zorder window until that window's own tick is on screen - the compositor routing the press, the client drawing, the client PRESENTING (WM_ACTION_PRESENT, new in M117) and the compositor compositing that rectangle. The number a person feels when they click something. Polled with schedule() like the input_to_photon rows, so the observer competes the same way: measured 63-87 ms worst of three across the graded boots that landed it, against 10-38 ms for the cursor alone in the same boots, and most of the difference is the full frame a press that raises a window costs. Six boots in between read 734-751 ms - the ticks arriving on the 1 s safety net, with a trace showing the client's presents never reaching the compositor - and stopped doing so once every client presented its first frame at startup; see the M117 entry, which records that as a mechanism not yet understood. The ceiling covers the I/O APIC path, which costs 2x and read 212 ms for one press in `--full`; on the default path the worst of three has been 62-87 ms in every boot since. `measured` is the 2x path's number, because a ceiling is set against the worst a good run does. Before M117 the client's drawing waited on the compositor's 100 ms fallback poll; that poll is a 1 s safety net now, so a compositor that stopped honouring presents lands here at several hundred milliseconds, and the ceiling is set to catch that rather than to police the 65.

M117: the CPU ticks the compositor, a wm_zorder window and three clocks used over two seconds with nothing touching the machine, as a percentage of the window - from the tasks' own user+sys tick counters, NOT the BSP idle count, which reads near 100% busy throughout a battery whatever the desktop does (see the [m117] block in kernel.c). Before M117 every wmclient loop yielded instead of blocking, so one open window used every tick it was offered. Three clocks redraw and present four times a second each, and the compositor polls the mouse every 10 ms, so the honest floor is not 0; the ceiling is where a client that has gone back to spinning cannot hide. Measured 2 on the first graded boot with the per-task version; a single spinning client would read 50 or more.

M117: the longest wait between two frames of one window animation, one row per animation, from the compositor itself. This replaces a rule that had failed a boot on any composite longer than FRAME_BUDGET_MS (16 ms) since M61 - a number that excluded the yields, the other tasks and the wait for the tick, i.e. everything a person waits through between two frames. On the DESKTOP, measured with this same report built into HEAD before M117: 3-5 frames per 140 ms animation and a longest gap of 60-100 ms, every time; after M117, 4-7 frames and 40-50 ms typical, one in seven at 90. That desktop number is graded where it belongs, by the input suite's window_animations_stay_smooth, on a quiet desktop. This row runs inside the boot battery, where animations happen beside kernel test tasks polling the framebuffer and, in M69's loaded phase, beside CPU-bound tasks spun on purpose: 66 animations in one battery ran 20-70 ms with a handful at 110-120 and one at 170 (the [m43] launcher test). The ceiling is set above that, so what this row catches is an animation that stops - a compositor that no longer wakes for its frame - rather than the desktop's smoothness, which the suite grades against HEAD's own numbers.

M199: the mean lateness of twenty 3 ms sleeps, from the TSC. Before M199 every deadline was noticed on the first 100 Hz tick after it passed, AND an idle core whose own tick woke the sleeper went back to halting until the next tick - so on one CPU a 3 ms sleep took about 15. The one-shot LAPIC timer each core arms for its earliest deadline, plus a tick that looks at what it just woke, bring it to microseconds on hardware; under QEMU on macOS the host delivers the timer about 2 ms late, which is most of what this row measures. Measured with the timer but without the tick fix: 5526. The ceiling sits between the two so either regression fails here rather than feeling slow.
